1.summary: Jerusalem is pictured as a widow weeping alone, abandoned by her lovers and stripped by her enemies, until she herself speaks, confessing her sin and begging Yahweh to see her sorrow.
1.lookfor: Watch the refrain that no one comforts her, the moment the voice switches from a narrator to Zion herself, and what she asks of passers-by and of God.

names.name: Zion
names.gloss: The hill of the temple, and a poetic name for Jerusalem and its people.

insights.title: How!
insights.body: The book opens with eikhah, How! (1:1), a cry used at the start of funeral laments. It became the book's Hebrew title. The same word opens chapters 2 and 4.

insights.title: An alphabet of grief
insights.body: Chapter 1 is an acrostic: each of its 22 verses begins with the next letter of the Hebrew alphabet. Chapters 2, 3 and 4 follow the same pattern, and chapter 5 has 22 verses without it. The form may express completeness, grief from A to Z, or give order to chaos; it cannot be seen in translation.

insights.title: Laments for fallen cities
insights.body: Ancient Mesopotamia had a tradition of poems mourning destroyed cities, such as the Lament over the Destruction of Ur, in which the city's goddess weeps. Lamentations shares some features, like the city pictured as a weeping woman. But here the city confesses her own sin and the destroying God is also the one addressed in prayer.

insights.title: No one to comfort
insights.body: The phrase no one to comfort her runs through the chapter (1:2, 1:9, 1:16, 1:17, 1:21). Her lovers, the allies Judah trusted, have betrayed her (1:2, 1:19). Isaiah 40 opens with the answer this chapter longs for: Comfort my people.

insights.title: Nations in the sanctuary
insights.body: Zion has seen the nations enter her sanctuary, whom God had forbidden to enter his assembly (1:10). The law excluded certain foreigners from Israel's assembly; now pagan soldiers walk into the holiest place. Psalm 79 laments the same desecration.

insights.title: Is it nothing to you?
insights.body: Zion asks those passing by whether any sorrow is like hers (1:12). Christians have long read this verse in Holy Week as words fitting Jesus on the cross, and Handel set it in Messiah. In its own setting it is the cry of a ruined city to indifferent travelers.

insights.title: The winepress
insights.body: The Lord has trodden the virgin daughter of Judah as in a winepress (1:15). Treading grapes, with juice running like blood, was a vivid picture of slaughter. Isaiah and Revelation use it for God's judgment on the nations.

insights.title: Yahweh is righteous
insights.body: In the middle of her pain Zion says, Yahweh is righteous; for I have rebelled (1:18). She confesses, yet still asks God to look at her suffering (1:20). Can a sufferer admit fault and still protest the depth of her pain?

2.summary: The poet describes the Lord acting like an enemy, tearing down Zion's walls, temple, king and priests, weeps over children dying of hunger in the streets, and urges Zion to cry out to God for them.
2.lookfor: Watch the long list of things God has done in 2:1-9, the poet's own grief in 2:11-13, the false prophets, and Zion's bold question to God at the end.

insights.title: God as enemy
insights.body: The Lord has become as an enemy (2:5). Verse after verse makes God the subject of destruction: he has swallowed, thrown down, cut off, burned and bent his bow (2:2-4). The poem does not blame Babylon; it names God as the one behind the disaster.

insights.title: His footstool
insights.body: God did not remember his footstool in the day of his anger (2:1). The ark of the covenant, or the temple where it rested, was pictured as the footstool of God, who sat enthroned above. Even that he let go.

insights.title: The measuring line
insights.body: Yahweh has stretched out the line to destroy the wall (2:8). Builders used a measuring line to plan construction; here it marks out what to tear down. The prophets had used the same image for the coming judgment on Jerusalem.

insights.title: My liver poured out
insights.body: The poet says, My liver is poured on the earth (2:11). Hebrew located deep emotion in the inner organs, liver and bowels, as English uses the heart. The grief is for children fainting in the streets and asking their mothers for grain and wine (2:12).

insights.title: Prophets who did not expose sin
insights.body: Zion's prophets saw false and foolish visions and did not uncover your iniquity (2:14). Had they named the sin, the captivity might have been reversed. The verse echoes Jeremiah's long struggle with prophets of peace.

insights.title: The perfection of beauty
insights.body: Passers-by mock: Is this the city that men called The perfection of beauty, the joy of the whole earth? (2:15). The titles come from Zion psalms that celebrated the city as God's beautiful, unshakable dwelling. Their hymns are thrown back at them.

insights.title: What God said long ago
insights.body: Yahweh has done what he planned, fulfilling his word commanded in the days of old (2:17). This most likely points to the covenant curses in Leviticus and Deuteronomy. The disaster is not random but the threatened outcome of a broken covenant.

insights.title: Look, Yahweh, and see
insights.body: Zion asks God to look at what he has done: should women eat their children, and priests and prophets be killed in the sanctuary? (2:20). The question is left unanswered. What does it mean that Scripture includes such raw words addressed to God?

3.summary: A man who has suffered God's blows describes his darkness in detail, then remembers that Yahweh's loving kindness and compassion never fail, urges patient waiting and repentance, and prays for rescue and justice.
3.lookfor: Watch how the speaker's complaint in 3:1-18 turns in 3:21, the reasons for hope in 3:22-39, the move from I to we, and the prayer from the pit at the end.

insights.title: A triple acrostic
insights.body: Chapter 3 has 66 verses: three verses begin with each letter of the Hebrew alphabet in turn. It is the longest and most intricate poem of the book and stands at its centre. Its tight form frames its message of hope in the middle of chaos.

insights.title: Who is the man?
insights.body: I am the man who has seen affliction (3:1). Jewish and Christian tradition often heard Jeremiah, whose sufferings in pit and prison are echoed in 3:53-55. Others read the man as an everyman figure, a personification of the community, or even a king. Who speaks here, and could more than one reading be right?

insights.title: Images of attack
insights.body: The speaker describes God as a jailer who walls him in (3:7), a bear and a lion lying in wait (3:10), and an archer who uses him as a target (3:12). Job uses many of the same images. The language is the vocabulary of lament, honest about feeling hunted by God.

insights.title: New every morning
insights.body: Yahweh's loving kindnesses mean we are not consumed; they are new every morning; great is your faithfulness (3:22-23). Loving kindness is hesed, God's loyal covenant love, and faithfulness is emunah, reliability. A few ancient versions read 3:22 as Yahweh's loving kindnesses never cease. These verses inspired the hymn Great Is Thy Faithfulness.

insights.title: Yahweh is my portion
insights.body: Yahweh is my portion, says my soul (3:24). The priests and Levites received no land; God himself was their portion. With the land lost, the speaker claims the same inheritance.

insights.title: Give the cheek
insights.body: Let him give his cheek to him who strikes him (3:30). The verse counsels patient endurance of suffering while waiting on God (3:26-29). Isaiah's servant gives his cheek to those who strike, and Jesus teaches turning the other cheek.

insights.title: Not willingly
insights.body: For he does not afflict willingly, literally from his heart (3:33). The Lord will not cast off forever and will have compassion (3:31-32). The centre of the book holds together God's sovereignty over disaster (3:37-38) and his deep unwillingness to cause grief.

insights.title: From the lowest pit
insights.body: Enemies threw the speaker into a pit and set a stone on him; waters closed over his head (3:53-54). From the lowest dungeon he called on God's name, and God said, Don't be afraid (3:55-57). Jeremiah's cistern, Jonah's deep and Psalm 88 use the same images.

4.summary: The poet contrasts Jerusalem's past splendor with the horrors of the siege, blames its prophets and priests, mourns the capture of the king, and announces that Zion's punishment is complete while Edom's is coming.
4.lookfor: Watch the contrasts between before and after, the comparison with Sodom, the treatment of the priests, and the final word to Edom.

names.name: Edom
names.gloss: Judah's neighbor to the south-east, which rejoiced at Jerusalem's fall.

names.name: Uz
names.gloss: A land linked with Edom, Job's homeland.

insights.title: Gold grown dim
insights.body: How the gold has become dim! (4:1). The poem is built on contrasts: gold now dull, precious children treated like clay pots (4:2), people raised in purple now clinging to rubbish heaps (4:5). The sacred stones lie scattered in every street.

insights.title: Jackals and ostriches
insights.body: Even jackals nurse their young, but Zion's people have become cruel like the ostriches (4:3). Ancient people thought the ostrich careless with its eggs, as Job describes. Famine has broken even parents' care for their children (4:4).

insights.title: Worse than Sodom
insights.body: Jerusalem's punishment is greater than Sodom's, which was overthrown in a moment (4:6). Sodom's end came instantly; Jerusalem suffered a long siege. The comparison also recalls the prophets' charge that Jerusalem's leaders had become like Sodom.

insights.title: Nobles or Nazirites
insights.body: Her nobles were purer than snow (4:7). The Hebrew word, nezireha, can mean her princes or her Nazirites, people consecrated to God. Either way, those once radiant are now blacker than soot, skin shrivelled to the bone (4:8).

insights.title: Better the sword
insights.body: Those killed by the sword were better off than those killed by hunger (4:9). The poem records the worst horror of the siege, women boiling their own children (4:10). It states it soberly as the fulfilment of the covenant curse.

insights.title: Unclean!
insights.body: Prophets and priests, stained with the blood of the righteous, wander like blind men and people shout at them, Unclean! Go away! (4:14-15). This was the cry the law required of a person with a skin disease. Those who were to guard holiness are treated as defiled.

insights.title: The Lord's anointed captured
insights.body: The breath of our nostrils, the anointed of Yahweh, was caught in their pits (4:20). This is King Zedekiah, captured as he fled. Before that, the people had watched in vain for a nation that could not save (4:17), most likely Egypt.

insights.title: The cup passes to Edom
insights.body: The cup will pass through to you also, daughter of Edom (4:21). Then comes the first clear word of hope in the poem: your punishment is accomplished, daughter of Zion (4:22). Isaiah 40 opens with the same announcement that Jerusalem's term is served.

5.summary: The community prays together, asking Yahweh to remember their disgrace under foreign rule, confessing their sin, and pleading to be restored, while fearing he has rejected them.
5.lookfor: Watch the details of daily hardship, the line about fathers and children, the confession of 5:16, and how the book ends.

insights.title: Twenty-two lines, no acrostic
insights.body: Chapter 5 has 22 verses, matching the alphabet, but they do not follow its order. It is also shorter and steadier in rhythm, more like a communal lament psalm. Some see the collapse of the acrostic as fitting a prayer from people whose world has fallen apart.

insights.title: Paying for water and wood
insights.body: We have drunk our water for money; our wood is sold to us (5:4). Under occupation, basic resources that families once took freely from their own land had to be bought. Princes are hung up and elders dishonored (5:12), and young men carry millstones like slaves (5:13).

insights.title: Egypt and Assyria
insights.body: We have given our hands to the Egyptians and to the Assyrians for bread (5:6). Giving the hand means making a treaty or submitting. The verse may recall Judah's long history of leaning on the great powers, or describe its present dependence; Assyria may stand for whoever ruled Mesopotamia.

insights.title: Bearing the fathers' sins
insights.body: Our fathers sinned and are no more; we have borne their iniquities (5:7). Yet the same prayer says, Woe to us, for we have sinned! (5:16). The community holds together inherited judgment and its own guilt, the tension Jeremiah and Ezekiel address.

insights.title: Foxes on Mount Zion
insights.body: Mount Zion is desolate and foxes, or jackals, walk on it (5:18). The Talmud tells how Rabbi Akiva laughed on seeing a fox come out of the ruined Holy of Holies after the Romans destroyed the second temple. He reasoned that since this prophecy of ruin had come true, the prophecies of restoration would come true as well.

insights.title: Turn us, and we will be turned
insights.body: Turn us to yourself, Yahweh, and we will be turned. Renew our days as of old (5:21). Return to God is asked for as his gift. In the synagogue this verse is sung as the Torah scroll is returned to the ark.

insights.title: An ending without resolution
insights.body: The book ends: you have utterly rejected us, you are very angry against us (5:22). The Hebrew may be a statement or a fearful question, unless you have rejected us. In public reading, Jewish custom repeats 5:21 after it so as not to end on despair. Why might Scripture let a book end with the question still open?

insights.title: A throne that remains
insights.body: You, Yahweh, remain forever. Your throne is from generation to generation (5:19). With the earthly throne fallen (5:16) and the temple mount empty, the prayer rests on the one throne that has not fallen. It is the theological ground for asking God to remember.

intro.who: The Hebrew text names no author; the Greek Septuagint and Jewish tradition in the Talmud credit Jeremiah, who was known for laments. Many modern scholars think one or more poets in Judah wrote the five poems, perhaps not Jeremiah, since their style and outlook differ in places from his book.
intro.when: The poems describe the siege and burning of Jerusalem by Babylon in 587/586 BC and its aftermath, and were most likely written soon after, before the return from exile in 538 BC.
intro.why: Five carefully crafted poems give voice to grief over the ruined city, confess the sin that led to it, protest the scale of suffering, and keep praying to the God who struck the blow; Jewish communities read them each year on the fast of the ninth of Av.
